title: Forgiveness of Heart-Impurity and the Flight to Christ
english: Especially regarding Christ according to the economy; and that there is no deceit in his mouth is likewise to be understood as the fact that he has not possessed deceit. For there is no deceit in the mouth of the Word, being true and unsearchable.

Glancing from the true light in the day, I ran and in this day I cried out to you, praying [Ps 31:3]. Since I did not fall silent from this cry due to inattention, my bones were struck, both the strong and the soft of the dogmas, which are called my bones. And he means by saying these things the falling away, that his bones are becoming old, but are not old by nature.

And in those things that lead forward it is said, as in many places of the Scripture, that the punishing power of God is called his hand [Ps 31:4]. That this lies heavily upon him day and night—that is, he says continuously—is because of the change that comes upon the hand. The Savior interpreted the cares of life, both the pleasure and the thorns of deceit of this age. And if one is pierced by such a thorn, he is immediately turned into misery. It must be understood what one becomes miserable through change and turning, not being such by nature. The word means the wretched and the pitiable. And to be pierced by a thorn signifies not being such by nature, but it approaching from without. 'I was turned into misery' through repentance and through the instructive admonishment of the Lord; for the Lord loves whom he disciplines, but he scourges every son whom he does not receive [Heb 12:6]. Let us know in the Kings who endured because of this sin, being disciplined by the Lord because of his former righteousness, so that, having been freed from that sin and the punishment through it, he might take back his former health [1 Kings 15:3-5].

He who has fallen into sin, if he wishes to work it, provides a cover and hides it; but he who has hated it makes it manifest to the one who is able to heal through confession, declaring it [Ps 31:5]. But he also reveals the lawlessness appropriate to this; for the sight of sin is lawlessness; for everyone who acts lawlessly sins, though not everyone who sins acts lawlessly. It can be said by analogy, especially because everyone who does sin also does lawlessness, and lawlessness is sin. But having spoken truly, 'I confessed my sin against myself' [Ps 32:5] which I have done...

I did not ask for more lawlessness than what I had; for God has forgiven not only this but also the impiety of the heart. And impiety of the heart is able to be the dissatisfaction of providence occurring to many through the irregularity of things as they seem.

If even the righteous cleanse themselves from practical lawlessness (Ps 31:6a), they still often have impure thoughts from the aforementioned impiety of the heart. Even if those who pray do not have [thoughts] concerning lawlessness, they will pray concerning impiety, asking for its forgiveness in a favorable time. And a favorable time of prayer concerning the aforementioned forgiveness is when one cleanses himself from practical filthiness. And just as one who is wounded in a small scratch will not demand a physician's treatment, but having the whole body intact, only suffering in that single scratch, so no one filled with the guilt of actions will pray concerning the purity of thoughts, but only every righteous person.

When a flood of many spiritual waters comes (Ps 31:6b), having had a spring of water within himself changing into eternal life—that is, the waters vanishing all sins and the impiety of the heart upon them—impiety and lawlessness will not approach the one who has prayed for them.

He who says these things thinks he finds deliverance from the standing affliction in no other way than by fleeing to Christ (Ps 31:7). Just as righteousness and wisdom [are], so also is the joy of the diligent Jesus. For he says to Him as our joy: 'Deliver me from those pursuing me; for lawless demons and evil men pursue me; for I will be persuaded that nothing evil [can happen], You saving me.'

That is, not having cast away acting logically, you do not fall into an irrational state (Ps 31:9), such that through being headstrong you become like a mule because of being deficient toward evils; for such an impulse does not have understanding. The prophet says toward God: [He brings] those who have become like horses because of being skittish and unruly, and a mule, hard-mouthed, subduing their bits with nails and drawing them with Your suitable bridle, with which You lead them under Your yoke. The compliant and gentle ones approach God by a voluntary impulse, but those previously mentioned as horses and mules because of the lack of understanding...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Straightness of the Word and the Nature of the Heavens
english: Having become subject to the aforementioned necessity of the afflictions, they will be drawn toward you (Ps 32:1). Those who have accomplished an ethical life are righteous, rejoicing in the Lord, and it is necessary that those who flee from all the crookedness of false doctrine be upright. For it is fitting to praise God with these, since praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner (Ps 32:2).

Confession and here thanksgiving are expressed. This ought not to be made on a lyre. And if the body is a lyre, the stretched strings are none other than the senses; for being struck by divine hearing, they perceive the hearing and the heavens and those in them, seeing them as to marvel at the Creator, and using the other senses praiseworthy, we confess to the Lord rhythmically and harmoniously with this lyre. But if one should conceive the soul as a lyre, its powers—which are the mnemonic, the assentive, the productive, and others according to reason—being struck like strings by the mind musically, will confess to the Lord. Musicians say there is a difference between the psalmtery and the lyre, such as this: they say the lyre is composed of the lower parts, while the psalmtery is from the upper parts with the strings, and it is more straight through strings. Since the soul is given as lyres, the spirit of man, which is in it, is perhaps something other than the mind, is a psalmtery, singing not to anyone else but to God. For we use right thoughts and with our own spirit we receive the Holy Spirit, and we sing victoriously in a ten-stringed psalmtery. And perhaps from the ten strings its perfection is shown. For such a number is found continually being hymned in the Scriptures. And God used only ten general terms for the high priest Moses, and the people are commanded to offer ten.

He who hastens to praise God through all things and through voice will sing to God a new song (Ps 32:3), saying an anthem kindred to the new covenant and the newness of the Spirit, so that he might praise God not only with lyre and psalmtery but also with voice. And he wishes to sing praiseworthy with a shout of triumph; for the shout is a voice. He who makes a shout without distraction and without insignificance against the conquered enemies, then he says, 'You have sung well,' while those having conquered say, 'Shout!'

Because of the enemies. The word of the Lord, which he gives to those pursuing knowledge, is straight and not a crooked deception (Ps 32:4). Moreover, the workers perform the appropriate things for this word, being fulfilled in faith; and the works which the word of God performs are in faith, that is, they are firm and unshakeable, and the word by which he governs and provides is straight.

If someone were to call the word of God a straight word, the works he performed in this word, being fulfilled in faith, would be easy; for the paradoxical works of Jesus are his works according to the faith of those, becoming [things] for them: 'Let it be done to you according to your faith' (Ps 32:5). He himself is God, or his straight word, accepting judgment in that he must avenge the virtues being insulted by the wicked, but loving mercy, helping those being led to judgment by his own goodness. For if he were to observe all their works, no one would be able to endure. Therefore, even before judgment, he loves mercy. For if it were not so, all would suddenly be lost.

The heavens were made thin, having the most corruptible nature (Ps 32:6); for such is the nature of the heavens. But when taken allegorically, of all those who think upon the image of the so-called heavenly, their firm grip and stability becomes [theirs] through the word of the Lord, and their power, by which they are able, is not produced by anything else but by the Holy Spirit. And by this spoken word, pious men discourse that the Holy Spirit is the creative [force].

Just as water held in a skin or in another vessel is not permitted to pour out outside of the container holding it, so the vastness of the sea's water is limited by a certain boundary, not being allowed to exceed the appointed rivers. For if it did not hold back by the command of God, it would have overflowed the whole earth. But stop, unless even this is made clear: since, calling the water of the sea, he pours it out upon all the earth through the rains, his command, practicing justice, makes the water ethereal, as if composing a cloud of mists to be carried over the earth. Allegorically, the life of men is often called a sea.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Divine Providence and the Folly of Human Strength
english: Because of the still and salty nature of the waters upon the earth, the sea, which is called the abyss, gathers them together—not as if they were scattered by a storm—as if in a skin, so that the Savior might take up the body to become calm and drinkable. He places them in the abysses of treasuries.

Nothing in creation is carried out disordered; for as a seed is held in its own treasuries by its own will, so it is released and held as it seems fit to it. It is said, moreover, that He brings the winds out of the treasuries, not by their own impulse, these being carried, but by the will of the Creator, sometimes closing them and sometimes bringing them out. But He also opens the treasury of the good heaven and gives rain to the seed of the earth, just as a seed is held, and He holds the rain by closing the heaven, as regarding the prophet Elijah. And the abysses, because they are not able to harm through the unlimited multitude of the waters, are placed in treasuries, enclosing them, so that if anyone wishes to use them, it is as is profitable according to the season (Ps 32:7).

It is also possible for the ungraspable of His thoughts and the unsearchable of His judgments, which happen to be abysses, to be placed in the hidden treasuries of knowledge and of wisdom, so that no one might attain to this from himself unless God should grant it (Ps 32:8-9). Since they came into being by His speaking and were created by His commanding, let them be shaken by Him; for it belongs to the Creator to change things toward the good (Ps 32:11a). 'They came into being' signifies the essence of those things regarded as being, and 'they were created' signifies the adornment having come into being after the essence. If all things came into being and were created by the speaking and commanding of God, then no one other than the creative Word spoke and commanded; and this is the Son of God.

And elsewhere it is said: 'For who has counseled that God the Holy should scatter?' (Ps 32:11b). Just as in other places it is said of God in a human way—as having hands and eyes and other things—so also He speaks of His heart, meaning His deliberative and intellectual energy. The thoughts of this energy, being unlifted and certain, extend from generation to generation, that is, through all the generations.

Divine thoughts remain as a conviction. Perhaps he did not cast thoughts upon the generation of the circumcised, but he casts these upon the generation from the believing Gentiles; for he has not called out against others, but against those in whom the shadows of the circumcised are hidden.

They inhabit the earth, not humans alone, but also invisible spirits and the other mortal animals (Ps 32:14b). The care of God, overseeing all, extends to everyone upon the earth, bringing them out from his aforementioned dwelling-place.
Since God understands not only the things accomplished but also the intention from which these things are activated (Ps 32:15b), it is said that he sees not, but understands all their works.

For that a king is not saved by much strength, you shall learn from history (Ps 32:16-17a); Pharaoh did not have a great array, but God cast his armor and his strength into the sea. And all history is full of such things. And he says that the one who is exceedingly strong will not be saved in the strength present to him; but having understood this, he speaks concerning Goliath. And if the allusion also indicates the god-fighter, no one shall be saved in a multitude of strengths of impious dogmas. The one called 'not strong' is to be found in Isaiah saying, 'Giant and strong,' but the god-fighter again by the same author: 'Giants come to fill my wrath, rejoicing.' And also in Genesis: 'And Nebroth was a mighty hunter before the Lord.' A horse is prepared for the day of battle, but the help is by the Lord (Prov 21:31).

Since the departing light from the eyes of God is life (Ps 32:19), the pious, participating in this and having hope upon the lion, would be saved from the death that follows wickedness, as if their souls were being made alive; but participating in the heavenly bread (and the word of God is not bread), they are nourished in famine. For famine he speaks of not the scarcity of edible foods, but the deprivation of divine teachings. Accompanying this is the saying, 'I will send famine upon the earth' (Amos 8:11), not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord.
